 Patrick Stewart, Prolific Shakespearean Actor, Dies at 86
 cuatower 
 November 17, 2026 
 0 
 Tweet 
 Image Courtesy of Variety 
 By Luis Zonenberg
 Hollywood has lost another legendary icon. Shortly after the death of the incredibly talented voice actor Eric Bauza, it was announced that Shakespearean actor Patrick Stewart died at the age of 86. Stewart was most famous for playing iconic characters like Captain Jean-Luc Picard from Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films. In light of his passing, I thought it was fitting to look back on his incredible career and see how much of an impact he had not just on the industry, but on his friends and family as well. 
 Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, in the West Riding of Yorkshire, England. His mother, Gladys Stewart, was a weaver and textile worker while his father, Alfred, served in the British Army during WWII, even aiding in the Dunkirk evacuation earlier that year. Stewart had two older brothers, but unfortunately grew up witnessing domestic violence at the hands of his father, likely as a result of Alfred’s PTSD following the end of the war. 
 Stewart’s father had a profound impact on his life, even shaping how he would get into character for his roles. In an interview with the American Theatre back in 2008, Stewart explained that, “My father was a very potent individual, a very powerful man, who got what he wanted. It was said that when he strode onto the parade ground, birds stopped singing. It was many, many years before I realised how my father inserted himself into my work. I’ve grown a moustache for Macbeth . My father didn’t have one, but when I looked in the mirror just before I went on stage I saw my father’s face staring straight back at me.” 
 Stewart attended Crowlees Junior and Infants School, a school affiliated with the Church of England in his hometown of Mirfield. He later attested that his acting career began there, recounting how his English teacher, Cecil Dormand, encouraged him to pursue a career in acting. In an interview with the BBC, he explained that Cecil “was the one that put a copy of Shakespeare in my hand [and] said, ‘Now get up on your feet and perform.’” 
 By the time he was 15, Stewart dropped out of school and began to participate in local theatre. During this time, he worked at a furniture store since this allowed him to attend dress rehearsals with few scheduling conflicts. He would later receive a grant from the West Riding Council to attend the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, becoming the first person who was neither an Oxford nor Cambridge graduate to receive a grant from the Council. 
 Stewart made his professional stage debut in 1959 playing Cutpurse in the classic play Cyrano de Bergerac at the Theatre Royal in Bristol. He would later become a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) in 1966, working with the company until 1982. Stewart did not initially have any interest in starring in film or television, preferring classic theatre to the more dramatic fictional narratives in the film industry. 
 In 1987, TV producer Robert H. Justman approached Stewart for a starring role in a Star Trek revival series after seeing him at a literary reading at UCLA. While Stewart was not aware of the immense cultural influence Star Trek had, signing a six-year contract for the show under the advice of his agent. They believed that the show would likely become a massive failure and once it was cancelled, Stewart could quickly return to performing on stage back home in England. 
 While Stewart did struggle adjusting to working on a film set, he grew to love the role after realizing how Shakespearean his character actually was. He later wrote , “There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that reminds me of numerous Shakespearean situations I’d been in onstage.” 
 “I should play Jean-Luc, I realised, as if he were a character in Henry IV, which is about brave men,” Stewart said.
 His positive experience working on Star Trek: The Next Generation prompted him to expand his career to working on other films and TV shows. He starred in TV-movie adaptations of Moby Dick and A Christmas Carol , even earning a Screen Actors Guild Nomination for his performance as Scrooge in the latter. He would even lend his voice to several animated films and TV shows like The Prince of Egypt and The Simpsons.  
 In the 1990s, Stewart accepted a key role in the X-Men film Twentieth Century Fox was producing with director Bryan Singer. Stewart agreed to portray the iconic Professor Charles Xavier, the humble but stern leader of the X-Men in the comics. The role would become one of his most famous, his name becoming synonymous with the role to the extent that he will be returning to it once more in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday . 
 Unfortunately, all good things must come to an end. Stewart passed away at his home in Los Angeles on Oct. 28, 2026. His publicist, Kelly Bush Novack, ultimately broke the news to the public. He had been under the care of his wife, Sunny Ozell, following a brief battle with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia. He is survived by his children, Daniel Stewart and Sophie Alexandra Stewart, both of whom he shared with his first wife, Sheila Falconer. 
 Since then, several people have offered their respects to Stewart and his family. Long-time friend and co-star, Ian McKellen, posted his condolences to his Instagram account. He wrote, “Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. 
 “Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love.” 
 Since then, more close friends and past co-stars have expressed their condolences. Star Trek: The Next Generation co-star Jonathan Frakes wrote , “There’s no one on this planet that I have acted with or directed more often than my late great friend Patrick Stewart. He will be with me forever. May he rest in Peace.” 
 Stewart leaves behind an incredible legacy not just on film, but on the stage as well. His work with the RSC ultimately paved the way for his career in Hollywood, redefining the way actors should prepare for a role. Audiences to this day love his portrayals of characters like Professor Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard; it will be hard to see audiences forgetting them anytime soon.
